interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the rule y = mx + c rewriting itself, with c at the y-axis crossing and m the climb for each 1 along, when you drag the c and m handles.
interactive.title: The m and c handles
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the squared grid from Gradient from two points. A straight line crosses the grid with two handles on it. The c handle is a round dot where the line crosses the y-axis, and it slides up and down the axis. The m handle sits on the line 1 along from that crossing, with a small step drawn under it, 1 across and m up or down, and dragging it up or down turns the line about the crossing. c snaps to whole numbers and m to halves. Above the grid the rule y = mx + c is written with the two numbers in, and it rewrites as either handle moves. c is the y at the crossing, because there x is 0, so m × x is 0 and only c is left. m is the climb for each 1 along, so it is the small step's rise. Where the line crosses the x-axis a small diamond marks it, the x-intercept, a different shape from the round c dot so the two are not mixed up. It sits where y = 0. When m is 0 the line lies level and the diamond goes, because a level line other than y = 0 never meets the x-axis. A test point can be dragged to any whole-number point. A readout puts its x into the rule, such as 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, and the point lights up "on the line" only when the answer is its y. On the parallel screen a faint copy of the starting line stays put while c slides, so you can see the gap between them stay the same all the way along. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Most puzzles show a rule or a line and three answers, and one asks you to drag the two handles until the line fits a rule. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the line and fills in the rule for that puzzle.
interactive.ignores: The handles snap to whole numbers for c and halves for m, and the test point to whole-number points, so the sums stay easy. m and c can be any numbers, and a line also passes through points with fractions between the grid points. The grid shows a short piece of each line, which carries on both ways. The resistor's readings and the bill are example values.

explain.text:
Any straight line that is not straight up has a rule, y = mx + c, that every point on it fits.[^1] m is the line's gradient,[^2] the climb for each 1 along, and c is where it crosses the y-axis.[^3] Take lesson 1's line through A (1, 3) and B (4, 9), whose gradient is 2. Going back 1 from A to x = 0 drops it by 2, to y = 1, so it crosses the y-axis at (0, 1). From there each 1 along adds 2, so at any x the line has climbed 2 × x above 1, and its height is y = 2x + 1. B fits, as 2 × 4 + 1 = 9. To test a point, put its x into the rule and see whether you get its y. (3, 7) is on the line, as 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, but (7, 3) is not, as 2 × 7 + 1 = 15.

Read the two numbers straight off the rule. Going 1 along adds 1 to x, so mx grows by m while c stays put, and y climbs m. That climb for each 1 along is the gradient, so the number multiplying x is m. c is the value of y where x = 0, because m × 0 is 0 and leaves y = c, so c is the y-coordinate where the line crosses the y-axis, the [[intercept]].[^3] Turn the line about its crossing and only m changes. Turn m to 0 and the line lies level: y = 0x + 1 is y = 1. Slide the crossing up or down and only c changes. Every point on the line moves by the same amount, so the new line runs alongside the old one and never meets it: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 are 4 apart at every x. Lines with the same m and different c are parallel. A line straight up, such as x = 2, has an undefined gradient,[^4] so there is no m and no rule of this form.

Before reading m and c, get the rule into the form y = …. y = 3 − 2x is y = −2x + 3, so m is −2, not 3. 2y = 3x − 8 is halved, every term, to y = 1.5x − 4, so m = 1.5 and c = −4. Engineering texts write the same rule as y = ax + b: Loughborough's HELM workbooks call a the gradient and b the vertical intercept,[^5] and the MCA's marine engineering syllabus calls y = ax + b the law of a straight line graph.[^6] The line also crosses the x-axis, and that point is easy to mix up with c. It is where y = 0. For y = 2x − 4, c is −4, at (0, −4), but 0 = 2x − 4 gives x = 2, so the line crosses the x-axis at (2, 0). That point is the [[x-intercept]]. It is a different point from c's crossing unless the line passes through (0, 0). Use 2 as c and y = 2x + 2 crosses the y-axis at (0, 2), 6 above the line's real crossing at (0, −4). A level line other than y = 0 never crosses the x-axis at all.

Lesson 1's example resistor, 10 V at 2 A and 25 V at 5 A, has a gradient of 5 V per A, its resistance,[^7] 5 Ω.[^8] Going back 2 A from 10 V drops 2 × 5 = 10 V, to 0 V at 0 A, so c = 0 and the rule is V = 5I, the y = kx of Proportional reasoning: a line through zero. **Every point on a line that is not straight up fits y = mx + c,[^1] where m, the number multiplying x, is the gradient[^2] and c, the value of y at x = 0, is where the line crosses the y-axis.[^3]**

analogy.text: A job priced as a call-out plus an hourly rate works like y = mx + c. The call-out is c, the charge before any time passes, and the hourly rate is m, added once more for each hour. Two firms with the same hourly rate but different call-outs stay the same amount apart however long the job runs, like parallel lines.
analogy.breaks: A bill starts at 0 hours and only goes up, so it never shows the line to the left of the y-axis or a falling line. If time is charged in whole hours, the bill goes up in steps, not along a line.

practice.text:
- Get the rule into the form y = mx + c, with y alone on the left. Divide every term when y has a number in front.
- Read m as the number multiplying x, with its sign, and c as the number on its own, with its sign.
- To draw the line, mark c on the y-axis, step 1 along and m up (down when m is negative), and mark a third point further on with the rule. Draw through them. If the three do not line up, m or c has slipped.
- To test a point, put its x into the rule and see whether you get its y.
- For the x-intercept, put y = 0 and solve for x. A level line other than y = 0 has none.

**Rule of thumb:** c is where x = 0, on the y-axis. The x-intercept is where y = 0, on the x-axis. Same m, different c: parallel lines.

**Worked example:** 3y = 6x + 9. Divide every term by 3: y = 2x + 3, so m = 2 and c = 3. Start at (0, 3) and step 1 along and 2 up to (1, 5). The rule puts a third point at (2, 7), as 2 × 2 + 3 = 7, and all three line up. The x-intercept: 0 = 2x + 3, so x = −1.5. Test (4, 10): 2 × 4 + 3 = 11, not 10, so that point is off the line. A parallel line through (0, −1) is y = 2x − 1.

**Common mistakes**
- Using the x-intercept as c. For y = 2x − 4, c is −4, though the line crosses the x-axis at 2. Only a line through (0, 0) has both at the same point.
- Taking the first number as m. y = 3 − 2x has m = −2.
- Dividing only some terms. 2y = 3x − 8 gives y = 1.5x − 4, not y = 1.5x − 8.
- Thinking lines that share c are parallel. They meet on the y-axis. Parallel lines share m.
- Swapping x and y when testing a point. In (7, 3), x is 7.
- Looking for y = mx + c for a line straight up. x = 2 has an undefined gradient.
